issues.item: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
issues.explanation: These items suggest an interpersonal/physical danger trauma pattern (monitoring dangerous people, avoiding exposed spaces due to vulnerability), which is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one unless additional assault/combat-type trauma is present.

issues.item: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, avoiding open spaces due to feeling physically vulnerable suggests a different threat context (e.g., assault, combat, public attack) and is not clinically well integrated with the other selected items, which are grief-related. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, 'Avoid Positive Feelings' and 'Avoid Grief Reminders' are coherent with bereavement-related PTSD, but 'Avoid Open Spaces' pulls toward a conflicting trauma/symptom pattern that is hard to explain from the provided formulation and item set.

vignette: Arthur Vance had been in his studio until the phone rang. The call came on a Tuesday, just past dawn, carrying the flat, clinical tone of the state police. His younger brother, Elias, had hydroplaned off the interstate during a sudden downpour and struck a concrete median. The world did not shatter so much as it went still. Arthur stood over his worktable, hands dusted with wet clay, listening to the dispatcher confirm what his stomach already knew. The suddenness of the crash left no room for preparation. There was no gradual farewell, only the abrupt absence where a person had been. In the months that followed, Arthur began to move through his days with a quiet, meticulous economy. He stopped keeping the wooden model boat Elias had built on the porch. He folded the winter scarf his brother always wore on his birthdays and packed it into a sealed bin in the garage. Anything that might pull his mind back to the accident became a boundary he drew carefully. When a police cruiser slowed near his driveway, Arthur would immediately close the blinds, his breath catching as the memory of the wet highway flooded his chest. He could not bear the sight of it. The silence in the house deepened, filled with the careful placement of objects away from his line of sight, a routine that took up as much energy as his daily work. By the following autumn, the habit of looking ahead had simply fallen away. Arthur no longer considered seasonal orders for his pottery studio, even though commissions had once flowed steadily. When Clara began discussing the possibility of a long-delayed trip to visit their daughter in Oregon, he changed the subject or retreated to the workshop. Making any arrangements for what came next felt like stepping onto thin ice. He kept his days unstructured, waking at the same hour, shaping clay, and returning to bed when the afternoon light grew heavy. The absence of future dates on the wall calendar was not a decision so much as a quiet erasure. Joy, when it arrived, was treated with the same guardedness. If a familiar joke made him laugh during a rare dinner with old friends, Arthur would quickly turn his attention to his glass, the sudden warmth in his chest feeling unfamiliar and precarious. He had come to believe that comfort was a trap, that allowing himself to feel settled might invite another kind of loss. The laughter would stop, his shoulders would tighten, and he would focus on the cool weight of his mug, pushing the feeling away as though it were a sudden draft that could snuff out a flame. It was not that he could not feel pleasure, but that he could not let it linger. The quiet accumulation of his precautions had narrowed his world to a single, safe present. Apprentices noticed how Arthur would abruptly wipe his hands clean whenever the kiln timer rang, a sound that had once signaled the successful completion of a glaze fire. He stopped attending the regional crafts fairs, preferring the isolation of his own bench. Clara learned to speak in careful tones, aware that any mention of tomorrow, any shared smile that lingered too long, would be met with a quiet withdrawal. What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning when he realized he could not remember the last time he had felt a genuine sense of ease. He was afraid he was building nothing but a monument to absence, and he hoped, perhaps for the first time, that someone might help him understand how to breathe again without the constant fear of another storm.
